Working with APIs is a fundamental skill for modern developers. Essentially, an API allows different software applications to communicate with each other. When you make an HTTP request, you are asking the API to send you data or perform an action. The response usually comes back in a simple text format called JSON, which is easy for both humans and machines to read.

However, before you can access most APIs, you often need to provide authentication, usually in the form of an API key. This key confirms that you have permission to use the service. As you work, you must also respect rate limits, which are rules that restrict how many requests you can make in a given time. Finally, good practice involves error handling—always checking the response code so you can gracefully manage problems, like a bad request or a server issue. This ensures your application remains stable and user-friendly.
